claims.text: Pristine, untreated Q235 steel in the as-received state is the material being studied.
The corrosion behavior of pristine Q235 steel is governed by the temperature-dependent integrity of a naturally forming iron-oxide passive film.
At approximately 25°C, Q235 steel forms a compact protective film that suppresses corrosion.
At approximately 80°C, the passive film on Q235 steel becomes porous or dissolves, accelerating corrosion-related degradation.
The proposed study exposes Q235 specimens to 3.5 wt.% NaCl while varying temperature and controlling humidity and chemical aggressiveness.
The principal temperature comparison is approximately 25°C versus approximately 80°C at constant NaCl concentration.
Passive-film density, porosity, and adhesion are the proposed structural mediators between temperature and corrosion.
At room temperature, kinetics favor formation of a uniform, adherent film composed mainly of Fe2O3 and Fe3O4.
An intact oxide film reduces ion transport and thereby limits corrosion.
Increasing temperature enhances passive-film porosity or dissolution.
Temperature-induced film degradation promotes aggressive-ion ingress, undermines protection, and accelerates corrosion.
Relative to specimens corroded at room temperature, specimens exposed at 80°C will exhibit lower passive-film integrity by electrochemical and surface measurements.
Relative to specimens corroded at room temperature, specimens exposed at 80°C will exhibit greater weight loss and higher corrosion-current density.
Q235 steel under room-temperature corrosion conditions typically develops a stable passive layer and experiences minimal corrosion.
The proposed effect is expected to apply under controlled 3.5 wt.% NaCl exposure over the stated temperature range.
Changes in pH, additional aggressive ions, or nonstandard humidity may alter passive-film behavior and the corrosion mechanism.
EIS, SEM, XPS, weight loss, and corrosion-current measurements can be used to compare film integrity and corrosion rate between the two temperature groups.
The proposed mechanism would be refuted if elevated-temperature specimens have film integrity and corrosion rates comparable to room-temperature specimens.
